meaning: A place full of busy, bustling activity; a crowded scene of constant industry (usually 'a beehive of activity').
note: Spelling variant only — normally set closed as 'beehive'. Not a corruption.

meaning: A subject one knows nothing about, or a person/matter that cannot be understood; also a matter that is finished and no longer open to discussion.
note: Two live senses: 'Physics is a closed book to me' (unknown/unintelligible) and 'that chapter is a closed book' (settled, over).

meaning: A thoroughly unsatisfactory or messy situation — said ironically, meaning the opposite of 'fine'.
note: The idiom is carried entirely by the sarcasm; 'a pretty pass' / 'a fine mess' are the same move.

meaning: A man with no fixed occupation or duties — a man of leisure with time on his hands.
note: 'At large' in the older sense of 'unattached, not assigned to a particular post', as in 'ambassador at large'. Often faintly mocking.

meaning: A sudden, brief, effusive outpouring of thanks or thankful feeling.
note: SUSPECT HEADING — this is not an idiom. It reads as an ordinary descriptive phrase lifted mid-sentence out of prose (the collocation is just 'a gush of' + emotion). Meaning given is compositional, not idiomatic.

meaning: A courageous, high-spirited, mettlesome man — one with pluck and liveliness who will not be cowed.
A supposed discovery that turns out to be illusory or worthless; by extension, a confused muddle.
note: Mares do not build nests — hence 'to find a mare's nest' = to be excited over nothing. The secondary 'tangled mess' sense is common in Indian and British usage.

meaning: A question open to debate and not settled; in modern American usage, a point of no practical consequence because it has already been decided or overtaken by events.
note: The two senses are nearly opposite and both are current — British/older 'arguable', American 'academic, irrelevant now'. Worth saying which a paper intends.

meaning: A task that is never finished — work deliberately undone as fast as it is done, and so drawn out indefinitely.
note: From the Odyssey: Penelope unpicked each night the shroud she wove by day, to postpone choosing a suitor.

meaning: Confused noise and bustle; clamorous, frantic and largely purposeless activity.
note: From Elizabethan stage directions marking off-stage battle — trumpet calls ('alarums') and soldiers rushing across ('excursions').

meaning: Exhausted, worn out, with nothing left; also (separately) fully committed, staking everything, and (British, of a price) all-inclusive.
note: Three distinct senses. The exam-deck sense for a bare 'all in' is almost always 'utterly tired out'; the poker 'stake everything' sense is the commonest modern one.

meaning: Scattered everywhere over a wide area; all over the place, far and wide.
note: American colloquial, often with an exasperated tone — 'I chased him all over hell's half acre'.

meaning: A bewildering mass of abbreviations, acronyms and initials that obscures rather than conveys meaning.
note: From the children's soup with pasta letters; typically used of bureaucratic or official jargon.

meaning: One of several resources, arguments or options a person has available to use — one weapon among many at one's disposal.
note: Usually met as 'another arrow in one's quiver' / 'the last arrow in the quiver' (the final resource left).

meaning: To support me — to stand behind me, endorse me, or provide me with money or authority.
note: SUSPECT HEADING — 'back me' is not an idiom on its own; it is the verb 'back' with a pronoun object, and the deck has probably truncated 'back (someone) up' or lifted the words out of a sentence. The idiomatic unit is 'back up' / 'back someone'.

meaning: Disreputable, worthless or dishonest people; scoundrels, rogues.
note: British and somewhat dated; the singular 'a bad hat' is the usual form.

meaning: Nonsense; especially insincere flattery or smooth talk intended to deceive.
note: American slang of the 1920s, of the same family as 'applesauce', 'baloney', 'soft soap'.

meaning: To be laid up with an illness ('down with flu'); in modern slang, to approve of, agree with, or be comfortable with something.
note: Two unrelated senses. The illness sense is the standard one; the 'I'm down with that' approval sense is recent American slang.

meaning: To be honest, fair and straightforward in one's dealings.
note: From the carpenter's square as an emblem of uprightness; also carries a Freemasonry association ('on the square' = a Mason).

meaning: To press or push downward with force; hence to apply oneself with concentrated effort, and (with 'on') to advance on someone or something in a purposeful, threatening way.
note: Also the specific obstetric sense, 'to push during labour'. The 'bear down on' approach sense is nautical in origin.

meaning: To win; to carry off the prize or the honours, to be adjudged the best.
note: From the palm branch awarded to victors in classical games — same image as 'yield the palm' (to admit defeat).

meaning: To endure or put up with something without giving way; to keep one's courage under strain.
note: SUSPECT HEADING — I do not think 'bear up with' is standard. It looks like a blend of 'bear up' (to keep one's spirits under trouble), 'bear up UNDER' (to withstand a strain) and 'bear with' (to be patient with someone). Meaning given covers the blend; the intended entry is most likely 'bear up under' or 'bear with'.

meaning: Irrelevant; off the point, not bearing on the matter in hand.
note: A variant of 'beside the point'; 'wide of the mark' is the near neighbour but leans more toward 'inaccurate' than 'irrelevant'.

meaning: A figure for misfortune, hardship or advancing age — the trouble that sooner or later treads on everyone.
note: SUSPECT HEADING — truncated. The idiom is the proverb 'the black ox has trod on his foot', i.e. misfortune (or old age) has overtaken him. Alone, 'black ox' is only the emblem, not a usable idiom.

meaning: Entered into a contest or argument with someone; tilted or jousted with an opponent, literally or in debate.
note: Inflected heading — the dictionary form is 'break a lance with'. Note the related 'break a lance FOR', which means to champion someone's cause rather than to fight them.

meaning: Violated the rules of grammar; spoke or wrote bad grammar.
note: Inflected heading; dictionary form 'break Priscian's head'. Priscian was the great Latin grammarian, so to injure him is to injure grammar.

meaning: To reprimand or scold sharply; also, to invoke something from above (to call down blessings or curses on someone).
note: The 'scold' sense is chiefly American (hence the noun 'a calling-down'); the 'invoke' sense is the older and more literary one.

meaning: Is in charge; gives the orders and makes the decisions.
note: SUSPECT HEADING — almost certainly a corruption of 'calls the shots'. As printed it would have to be read as the ordinary verb 'call for' (= demand, require), which does not fit a shot. Meaning given is that of 'call the shots'.

meaning: To win; to prevail, to gain the victory or have one's view accepted.
note: SUSPECT HEADING — corruption of 'carry the day'. The definite article is fixed in this idiom; 'carry a day' is not English.

meaning: The very best — an outstanding or excellent person or thing.
note: 1920s slang, usually 'the cat's whiskers'; sisters of 'the cat's pyjamas' and 'the cat's meow'. Often used sarcastically of someone with a high opinion of himself ('he thinks he's the cat's whiskers').

meaning: Turned pale or flushed — betrayed emotion by a change of complexion; in a separate military sense, deserted to the other side and changed allegiance.
note: Inflected heading, lifted in past tense; the dictionary form is 'change colour' (show emotion) or 'change one's colours' (switch sides). The two senses differ in number — singular 'colour' for the face, plural 'colours' for the flag — so the plural here points to the allegiance sense, though decks routinely use it for the blushing one.
